'''Antje Boetius''' (born 5 March 1967) is a German [[marine biology|marine biologist]]. She is a professor of [[geomicrobiology]] at the [[Max Planck Institute for Marine Microbiology]], [[University of Bremen]].<ref name="A">[http://www.mpi-bremen.de/en/Antje_Boetius.html Antje Boetius], profile at the University of Bremen webpage, retrieved 28 May 2010.</ref> Boetius received the [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Prize]] in March 2009 for her study of sea bed microorganisms that affect the global climate.<ref name="E">[http://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2008-12/df-t2l121108.php 2009 Leibniz prizewinners], Eurekalert, retrieved 28 May 2010.</ref> She has been the director of Germany's polar research hub, the [[Alfred Wegener Institute for Polar and Marine Research|Alfred Wegener Institute]], since 2017.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=Management – AWI|url=https://www.awi.de/en/about-us/organisation/management.html|access-date=20 March 2021|website=awi.de}}</ref> In May 2025 she became president and CEO of the [[Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute]].<ref>[https://www.mbari.org/news/mbari-names-antje-boetius-as-next-president-and-ceo/ News]</ref>

Boetius was the first person to describe [[anaerobic oxidation of methane]],<ref name="E" /> and believes the Earth's earliest life forms may have subsisted on [[methane]] in the absence of molecular oxygen (instead reducing oxygen-containing compounds such as [[nitrate]] or [[sulfate]]).<ref name="G">[https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2002/aug/09/research.highereducation Methane-Eating Life Form May Halt Global Warming], ''[[The Guardian]]'', published 9 August 2002, retrieved 28 May 2010.</ref> She has also suggested such life forms may be able to reduce the rate of [[climate change]] in future.<ref name="G" /> She is one of the laureates of the 2018 [[Environment Prize (German Environment Foundation)]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dbu.de/2547.html|title=German Environmental Prize goes to Marine Biologist Boetius and Leipzig Waste Water Experts|website=dbu.de|language=en|access-date=29 October 2018|archive-date=8 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210208212854/https://www.dbu.de/2547.html}}</ref> Boetius also won the [[Erna Hamburger|Erna Hamburger Prize]] in 2019.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Erna Hamburger 2019|url=https://www.epflwishfoundation.org/erna-hamburger-2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200924121250/https://www.epflwishfoundation.org/erna-hamburger-2019|archive-date=24 September 2020|access-date=20 March 2021|website=wishfoundation-2|language=en}}</ref>

==Career==
Boetius received her biology degree from the [[University of Hamburg]] in 1992.<ref name="J">{{cite web | title=Jacobs University Bremen: Prof. Dr. Antje Boetius | website=jacobs-university.de | date=12 June 2008 | url=http://www.jacobs-university.de/directory/aboetius/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080612102054/http://www.jacobs-university.de/directory/aboetius/ | archive-date=12 June 2008 | access-date=26 April 2022}}</ref> Prior to undertaking graduate research, she spent time at the [[Scripps Institution of Oceanography]] in Southern California, where she drew inspiration from marine microbiologists including [[Farooq Azam]].<ref name=":0" /> While at Scripps, Boetius worked with sediments collected from the [[Clipperton fracture zone|Clarion-Clipperton fracture zone]], examining the small seafloor animals (copepods, nematodes) therein,<ref name=":0" /> but ultimately decided to study even smaller organisms: microbes.

Boetius carried out her doctorate research in biology advised by [[Victor Smetacek]], working to create the field she ultimately wanted to study: deep-sea environmental microbiology.<ref name=":0" /> While working on her doctoral research, she undertook fourteen deep-sea expeditions across the [[Seven Seas]].<ref name=":0">{{cite book |last=Marlow |first=J. |editor1-last=Whitaker |editor2-last=Barton | title=Women in Microbiology | publisher=American Society of Microbiology | date=1 May 2018 | isbn=978-1-55581-953-8 | doi=10.1128/9781555819545 |chapter= Antje Boetius: exploring the living infinite | pages=9–18}}</ref> She earned a doctor of philosophy (PhD) from the [[University of Bremen]] in 1996,<ref name="J" /> publishing a dissertation titled "Mikrobieller enzymatischer Abbau organischer Substanzen in Tiefseesedimenten" (Microbial enzymatic degradation of organic substances in deep sea sediments).<ref>{{Cite thesis|title=Mikrobieller enzymatischer Abbau organischer Substanzen in Tiefseesedimenten.|publisher=[s.n.]|date=1996|place=S.l.|first=Antje|last=Boetius|oclc = 841757104}}</ref>

Boetius joined the [[Max Planck Institute for Marine Microbiology]] as a postdoctoral researcher, and became an assistant professor in 2001<ref name="J" /> and an associate professor in 2003.<ref name="J" /> Her research interests are in the marine [[methane cycle]], the ecology of chemosynthetic habitats, microbial processes of early diagenesis in deep-sea sediments, pressure and temperature effects on microbial processes, microbial symbiosis, [[geomicrobiology]] and the global [[carbon cycle]].<ref name="A" /><ref name="J" /> In addition to her role as Professor of Geomicrobiology, which she has held since March 2009,<ref name="CV">[http://www.mpi-bremen.de/en/Curriculum_Vitae_Antje_Boetius.html Antje Boetius] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719063647/http://www.mpi-bremen.de/en/Curriculum_Vitae_Antje_Boetius.html |date=19 July 2011 }}, curriculum vitae at the University of Bremen, retrieved 28 May 2010.</ref> she is also leader of the HGF-MPG Bridge Group on Deep Sea Ecology and Technology<ref name="CV" /> and leader of the "Microbial Habitat Group" that researches biogeochemistry, transport processes and microbial processes in benthic environments.<ref name="CV" /> She took over as director of the [[Alfred Wegener Institute for Polar and Marine Research|Alfred Wegener Institute]]<ref name=":2" /> in November 2017.<ref>PDF Curriculum Vitae available at: {{Cite web|title=Employees – AWI|url=https://www.awi.de/en/about-us/organisation/staff/antje-boetius.html|access-date=20 March 2021|website=awi.de}}</ref>

Boetius is also engaged in research and conversations around "issues of deep-sea ecosystems, biodiversity, and our vision of how to live with a future ocean".<ref name=":0" /> Recent projects examine the interplay between [[Deep sea mining|deep-sea mining]], ecology, and sustainability.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Ackerman">{{Cite web|last=Ackerman|first=Daniel|title=Deep-Sea Mining: How to Balance Need for Metals with Ecological Impacts|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/deep-sea-mining-how-to-balance-need-for-metals-with-ecological-impacts1/|access-date=20 March 2021|website=Scientific American|language=en}}</ref> Of deep-sea mining research published in the journal [[Science Advances]] in April 2020,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Vonnahme|first1=T. R.|last2=Molari|first2=M.|last3=Janssen|first3=F.|last4=Wenzhöfer|first4=F.|last5=Haeckel|first5=M.|last6=Titschack|first6=J.|last7=Boetius|first7=A.|date=1 May 2020|title=Effects of a deep-sea mining experiment on seafloor microbial communities and functions after 26 years |journal=Science Advances |language=en |volume=6 |issue=18 |article-number=eaaz5922 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.aaz5922 |pmid=32426478|pmc=7190355 |bibcode=2020SciA....6.5922V |issn=2375-2548}}</ref> Boetius has said "our experiment really shows that such physical processes will stop animals and microbes from returning to repopulate that habitat"<ref name="Ackerman"/> and has, relatedly, cited the need to "test if there are ways to make deep-sea mining somewhat sustainable, for example, by creating a protected area for each exploited area".<ref name=":0" />

==Personal life==
Boetius grew up in [[Frankfurt|Frankfurt, Germany]], and took frequent vacations to the seaside as a child.<ref name=":0" /> She spent time in [[Southern California]] while studying and working at [[Scripps Institution of Oceanography]].<ref name=":0" />

Mission Medico describe her interests as {{lang|fr|la bonne cuisine, le bon vin, la bonne compagnie, la bonne musique, la mode et la vie citadine}} ('Good food, good wine, good company, good music, fashion and city life').<ref>[http://www.ifremer.fr/medeco/equipe/boetius.htm Boetius], {{in lang|fr}} Mission Medico, retrieved 28 May 2010.</ref>

Her grandfather Eduard Boëtius worked as a navigator on the [[LZ 129 Hindenburg|Hindenburg zeppelin]] and was one of the few surviving crew members of the [[Hindenburg disaster|Lakehurst disaster]].<ref name="c708">{{cite web | title=Antje Boetius | website=Munzinger Biographie | url=https://www.munzinger.de/register/portrait/biographien/Antje%20Boetius/00/31568 | language=de | access-date=1 May 2025}}</ref>
